subject: history
chapter_title: Changing Traditions: An Overview of Three Orders and Cultural Change

concepts.title: The Frame of the Three Orders
concepts.definition: The unit opens the study of western Europe between the ninth and sixteenth centuries, where society was organised in three orders of clergy, nobility and peasants, tied by feudal bonds of land and loyalty under weak kings and strong lords.
concepts.key_idea: The three orders framed medieval life, and the chapter traces how their balance shifted with towns, trade and technology.

concepts.title: Changing Cultural Traditions: The Renaissance Frame
concepts.definition: From the fourteenth century, towns of Italy grew a distinct urban culture where humanism revived classical learning, art patronage flourished and the individual came to the centre, preparing the cultural changes called the Renaissance that this unit follows into the modern world.
concepts.key_idea: The Renaissance began as an Italian urban phenomenon with merchants and popes patronising artists, and printing spread its achievements across Europe.

concepts.title: Nomadic Empires and the Steppe Frame of the Unit
concepts.definition: The unit also signals the world of nomadic empires of the steppes, where Mongol conquests under Genghis Khan linked Europe and Asia, reminding readers that the settled three order society and the Renaissance towns coexisted with powerful nomadic neighbours.
concepts.key_idea: Comparing settled and nomadic worlds shows the variety of medieval political organisation beyond feudal Europe and Renaissance Italy.
